Step 1: The sales clerks in a bank can use their software frontend to receive the credit-scoring for a certain customer. 
This starts a process in the banking system which communicates with the agency in the background. 
This process sends a scoring request to the agency right after the beginning. 
Then, the Agency does a first quick scoring (level 1). 
This will often lead to an immediate result which is then returned directly to the banking system within seconds. 
The banking process presents the result to the clerk sitting at the frontend. 
Sometimes the scoring cannot be determined immediately and takes longer. 
In this case the agency informs the banking process of the delay and then starts the level 2 scoring (which can take up to a couple of minutes). 
After the scoring result is determined, the information is sent back to the banking process. 
The banking process displays a message to the clerk when he receives information about the delay to check again later. 
As soon as the result arrives, it can be seen at the frontend.
[Transition]: The agency’s completion of the credit‑scoring and return of the result (Process A) triggers the banking system’s workflow (Process B) to update the clerk’s interface and handle any required follow‑up actions.

[Transition]: Once the customer’s credit‑scoring outcome is finalized, the Payment Office triggers the weekly cycle by generating the vendor payment report, which is then automatically distributed to clients and routed to the Registry office and Accounts Receivable Department for invoice archiving and client billing.
Step 3: At the end of every week, the Payment Office of SSP generates a payment report and then pays the vendor.
This payment report is sent automatically to clients (including the payment invoice), also the payment office must send the payment report to both the Registry office and to the Accounts Receivable Department.
The Accounts Receivable Department generates the monthly invoice for clients, and then charges $35 per invoice notifying the client.
The Registry office selects the paper-based invoices that have been paid in order to archive the invoices per vendor and then per payment data; also, this office tracks down the payment.

Step 4: The reimbursement process within the ERICS company is started as soon as a reimbursement request is received.
After receiving the request a reimbursement contact is created.
Afterwards a beneficiary is chosen.
Then, a refund period is contract duration is determined.
Once this has been completed a check is done to see if a customer is part of a "Verband" or only has normal subsidiaries.
In the former case, the customer group association is selected.
In the latter case, customers are selected manually.
Once either of these two activities have been completed a threshold is set.
Once the refund period has ended, a credit note is printed and sent to the customer.
In the meanwhile a reimbursement is calculated and paid to the customer.
Once the payment has been made and the notification to the customer has been sent, the process ends.
[Transition]: The credit note issued to the client at the conclusion of ERICS’s reimbursement is forwarded to the SSP Mail Centre; upon receipt, the Mail Centre categorizes the invoice by staff member, thereby initiating the workflow of Process B.
Step 5: Once the Mail Centre office of SSP receives an invoice from the client, it categorizes the invoice by staff member.
Then, the invoice is forwarded to the Administration Department; this Department processes the Invoice (a complex process) and then puts all the invoices into a collection box.
At 10 am every workday, the Data Entry office takes the invoices and enters all data in the SAP system, another complex process.
Every hour the Mail Centre office reviews the system and forwards all new invoices for validation; the Validation office executes the big process of validating invoices.
At the beginning of every week, the Payment office executes the payment of every validate invoice, this is another big process.
After the payment, all invoices are archived by the Registry office.
[Transition]: After the Registry office archives the paid invoices, the client—now assured of payment receipt—is prompted to create a PayPal account to manage future online transactions, thereby initiating Process B.
Step 6: A client who wants to create a PayPal account first needs to determine the desired account type.
He should either select a personal account or a premium account.
Afterward, the client should enter login details, such as e-mail address and desired password, personal details, such as name and date of birth, as well as his telephone number and address.
Finally, the client needs to declare if he has been affiliated with any politically exposed person.
When the client clicks the create account button, the details will be sent to the PayPal system.
When a request is received, the system will validate the input fields.
If there are any invalid fields, the client will be notified and needs to correct them.
Otherwise, a welcome email will be generated and sent to indicate that an account has been created.
[Transition]: After the client’s PayPal account is successfully created and validated, the system initiates the subrogation workflow to determine whether any insurance claim can be recovered from the client.
Step 7: If an insurant could be possibly subrogated against, I get information about that. 
I check that case and if the possibility is really there, I send a request for payment to the insurant and make me a reminder. 
If recourse is not possible, I close the case. 
When we receive the money, I make a booking and close the case. 
If the insurant disagrees with the recourse, I'll have to check the reasoning of that. 
If he is right, I simply close the case. 
If he is wrong, I forward the case to a collection agency. It the deadline for disagreement is reached and we haven't received any money, I forward the case to the collection agency as well.
